intrinsic_value_estimate: Roughly $45–60 per share, central figure about $52. Method: owner earnings (reported earnings plus depreciation and amortization, less capital spending). 1987 owner earnings were $2.07–2.46 per share, midpoint about $2.25. If 1988 continued the 1987 trend, they would be about $2.55, but that is an assumption because 1988 figures are not in the packet. I valued these with growth that matches the past record (8–12% a year with no help from currency), using a 12% required return, which is management's own after-tax cost of capital. On that basis owner earnings are worth about 20–23 times. Cross-check: on the central case (10% growth, multiple falling to 15x over 10 years), buying at $46.56 returns about 11.6% a year. It fails the framework's explicit rule of buying below net working capital: net working capital is about $0.05 per share.
margin_of_safety: Thin. The price is about 10% below my $52 central figure. On 1987 numbers that is about 2–3 points a year of expected return above an assumed 9% Treasury yield, and the return falls below bonds if growth slows to 8% and the multiple drops back to the 1983–84 level of about 11–13x. The price gives no asset cushion. The safety comes from the franchise's durability: a very low chance that anything could drastically change the underlying value.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns exceptional returns on equity without relying on debt. In 1976–81 return on equity was about 20% with debt at 3.5–9% of capital, and it is now 27%.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Business analysis: return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: 12-year table in ar-1987: ROE 20.3–21.2% in 1976–79 at 3.5–6.3% debt to capital, 27.2% in 1987 with net debt at 15.3% of capital. 1987 pretax return on identifiable assets: international soft drinks 52%, all soft drinks 34%.

key_reasons.reason: It has a durable competitive advantage that is widening, built on brand, distribution and pricing power, with a long runway for growth abroad.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: Company brands hold more than 44% of world soft-drink volume, double the nearest competitor. Coke's US volume gain was over 60% of total US industry growth in 1986. Fountain sales outsell the nearest rival more than 2 to 1. International consumption per person is 16% of the US rate. US concentrate gross margin is about 63% (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings, and the business pays out most of what it earns while still growing.
key_reasons.evidence: 1987: net income $916M plus depreciation $153M less capital spending $300M gives about $770M of owner earnings. Over 1985–87 about $2.3B of $2.57B net income went to dividends and buybacks, while underlying earnings still rose from $678M to $916M.

key_reasons.reason: Management is able, has run the company since 1981, judges investments in terms of return on capital, and has created far more market value than it retained.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Management in place; each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1982, brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: About $2.0B retained in 1982–87 against about $13B of added market value. Return on retained capital was about 24%, against management's stated 12% cost of capital. The 1984–85 buybacks were made at about 11–15x earnings (ar-1986, ar-1987, prices).

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible for an outstanding business if the future develops much like the past, but it is not a bargain.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §5 Valuation as it evolved: outstanding business at a sensible price (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 19.2x 1987 EPS and about 21x owner earnings, or about 17–21x for the core business after setting aside the $2.3B of investments. The central case returns about 11.6% a year against an assumed bond yield of about 9%.

key_reasons.reason: The position should be large but below the 40% maximum. The chance of the underlying value being drastically impaired is very low, but the price gives little margin.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: Earnings rose steadily for 12 years and the 1985 formula change did not damage the brand, which counts toward high certainty. Against that, the trailing multiple is the highest since 1981 and the stock is near its 52-week high of $49.12 (prices).

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed. Returns come from the business compounding, and this would be a long-term holding.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 The market eventually confirms business success; §8 default holding period is forever (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: There is no announced transaction, so this is not a work-out. The ongoing 40M-share buyback and the policy of lowering the payout ratio toward 40% put more retained capital into a core business earning over 20% (ar-1987).

risks: Valuation: the thin margin of safety means a few years of slower growth or the multiple returning to 11–13x would produce returns below bonds.
Currency: part of the 1986–87 growth came from a weaker dollar (key currencies up 27% and 16%), and about 77% of soft-drink operating income comes from abroad.

Diversification relapse: in 1982–86 shares were issued to buy entertainment businesses that ended up earning about 3–4% on carrying value, far below the 12% hurdle. There is now about $1.2B of borrowing capacity that could fund another such move.
Off-balance-sheet leverage: CCE carries $2.72B of liabilities, contingent guarantees total $394M, and CCFC debt (about $300M) will be consolidated.
About $2.3B is in investments earning about 5% (CPE, bottlers), and Foods operating income fell sharply in 1987.
Stale data: no 1988 results are available, and the stock has risen from about $38 to $46.56 since year-end 1987.
Inflation, price controls and low margins in Latin America and other hyperinflationary markets.
what_would_change_my_mind: 1988 results showing earnings growth stalled, or that currency accounted for most of 1986–88 operating-income growth, so that underlying volume and price gains are well below 8%.
Evidence that share is being lost to the main competitor in US food stores, fountain, or the main international markets.
Management using its borrowing capacity for a large acquisition outside soft drinks, or issuing shares on terms that dilute value.
Meeting management and finding that 'shareholder value' is a slogan rather than a conviction, or that the reporting hides problems.
A substantially lower price (for example, back toward 12–15x earnings as in October 1987) would justify increasing the stake toward 30–40%.
A long-term Treasury yield well above 9% would remove the central case's return advantage.
sell_triggers: Lasting erosion of the competitive advantage: several years of falling worldwide or US share, or losing the ability to raise prices with inflation.
Capital allocation going badly wrong: retained earnings put into businesses earning below the 12% hurdle, or the $1 retained / $1 of market value test failing over a five-year period.
Leverage-funded diversification that pushes net debt to or above the 35% ceiling for purposes other than buybacks below value.
Evidence that management's integrity or candor is lacking (misleading reporting, accounting gimmickry).
Price alone is not a sell trigger for a permanent holding of an outstanding business (brk-letter-1983#2, brk-letter-1987#18).
